newsitem.title: AUSTRIA: Analysts in doubt as Creditanstalt deadline looms.
newsitem.headline: Analysts in doubt as Creditanstalt deadline looms.

text.p: As the clock ticked away for an Austro-Italian-German group to make a last-minute offer for privatisation candidate Creditanstalt, analysts on Friday were sceptical the group would come up trumps in time.

The group, which includes savings bank Die Erste, Austro-Italian insurer EA-Generali and Commerzbank of Germany, has until midnight Friday to present an offer for the government's 70 percent voting stake in the bank.
"People are very sceptical that there will be a speedy solution," said Gerhard Auer, Austria analyst at ICE Securities in London. "I think it's unlikely we'll see any result today."
A source near the consortium earlier on Friday said the group would make a statement later in the day outlining its stance, but said there would be no exact details.

Finance Minister Viktor Klima, in charge of the sale, has said he will reopen the six-year long privatisation process on Monday and will invite new bidders if the consortium, alienated by growing internal dissent, fails to comply with the deadline.

Analysts agreed that any delay in what is already Austria's longest-running privatisation saga would do little else but further damage the image of Creditanstalt, Austria's most traditional and second-largest bank.
"The bride is getting older and uglier with every day that passes by," said Gerhard Reisenberger, an analyst at ICI Group Sigeco in London. "I doubt anybody is really interested in this anymore."
The Vienna Bourse on Friday said it could not rule out a suspension of Creditanstalt's shares later in the day should the consortium make a price-sensitive statement.

Creditanstalt's common shares were down 7 schillings ($0.671) at 662 in early trade on the Vienna bourse, while the bank's preference stock -- 70 percent of which is held by the Republic of Austria, giving it 48.6 percent of the bank's base capital -- was down 4.70 at 479.30 schillings.
The preferred shares have lost as much as 23 percent over the past six months and are trading just above their year-low of 470.30 schillings, reached at the end of August.
A final offer by the consortium has been delayed by growing dissent among the group's members, particularly over Die Erste's plans to hold a majority of the proposed holding with Creditanstalt.
Die Erste is barely a third of the size of Creditanstalt, which has total assets of almost 700 billion schillings.

Austrian newspapers on Thursday reported Die Erste was ready to soften its stance and reconsider its demand for control of the holding after Commerzbank threatened to leave the consortium. The bank declined to comment on the reports.

"The exact shape of the consortium is unknown to this day," a source close to the consortium told Reuters on Thursday. "Either there is an offer and we'll have to clarify it or there won't be an offer." ($1=10.44 Schilling)
